Front: Ch 2: What does rough ER make that smooth ER does not?
Back: Membrane and secretory proteins — rough ER carries ribosomes; smooth ER makes lipids and steroids and detoxifies.

Front: Ch 2: Which organelle is the main site of steroid synthesis?
Back: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

Front: Ch 2: What does the proteasome do?
Back: Degrades proteins that have been tagged with ubiquitin.

Front: Ch 2: Which cytoskeletal element forms the cleavage furrow in cytokinesis?
Back: Actin microfilaments.

Front: Ch 2: What passes through a nuclear pore?
Back: RNAs and proteins moving between nucleus and cytoplasm, by selective transport.

Front: Ch 3: What is a nucleosome?
Back: About 150 base pairs of DNA wrapped around an octamer of histones (two each of H2A H2B H3 H4) with H1 outside.

Front: Ch 3: Heterochromatin versus euchromatin?
Back: Heterochromatin is condensed and transcriptionally silent; euchromatin is dispersed and active.

Front: Ch 3: What is a Barr body?
Back: The inactivated X chromosome — facultative heterochromatin in a female somatic cell.

Front: Ch 3: Which checkpoint does p53 control?
Back: The G1 checkpoint: it arrests the cycle for DNA repair and triggers apoptosis if repair fails.

Front: Ch 3: What do cyclins and CDKs do?
Back: Cyclin binds a cyclin-dependent kinase; the complex phosphorylates target proteins to drive the cell through a cycle phase.

Front: Ch 3: Give two structural differences between apoptosis and necrosis.
Back: Apoptosis shrinks the cell and keeps the membrane intact (apoptotic bodies, no inflammation); necrosis swells and ruptures the cell and inflames tissue.

Front: Ch 3: Meiosis I versus meiosis II in one line each?
Back: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (reductional); meiosis II separates sister chromatids (equational).

Front: Ch 3: What does the nucleolus make?
Back: Ribosomal RNA and ribosomal subunits.

Front: Ch 5: Which collagen type forms reticular fibers?
Back: Type III collagen.

Front: Ch 5: What is the main ground-substance GAG of loose connective tissue?
Back: Hyaluronan — unsulfated and the only GAG not attached to a core protein.

Front: Ch 5: Which cells store histamine and heparin?
Back: Mast cells.

Front: Ch 5: What does a plasma cell secrete?
Back: Antibody (immunoglobulin); it has an eccentric clock-face nucleus and a pale perinuclear Golgi halo.

Front: Ch 5: What produces the ground substance of connective tissue?
Back: Fibroblasts (and, in cartilage, chondrocytes) — they secrete proteoglycans and glycoproteins.

Front: Ch 6: How large is a white adipocyte?
Back: About 50–150 µm in diameter — large enough to be seen with a hand lens.

Front: Ch 6: Where is UCP1 and what does it do?
Back: In the inner mitochondrial membrane; it uncouples the proton gradient so energy is released as heat rather than ATP.

Front: Ch 6: What secretes leptin and what does it do?
Back: Adipocytes; it acts on the hypothalamus to reduce appetite.

Front: Ch 6: What does adiponectin do?
Back: Increases insulin sensitivity; its level falls in obesity.

Front: Ch 6: What activates hormone-sensitive lipase?
Back: Norepinephrine (from sympathetic nerves and the adrenal gland) and growth hormone; insulin inhibits it.

Front: Ch 6: Where is brown fat found in the newborn?
Back: Interscapular, axillary, perirenal, and along the great vessels.

Front: Ch 7: Which cartilage type has the most abundant collagen and the least proteoglycan?
Back: Fibrocartilage — type I collagen bundles with rows of chondrocytes and no perichondrium.

Front: Ch 7: Where is hyaline cartilage found?
Back: Articular surfaces, costal cartilage, nose, trachea, and the fetal skeleton.

Front: Ch 7: Where is elastic cartilage found?
Back: Auricle, external acoustic meatus, epiglottis, and Eustachian tube.

Front: Ch 7: Which cartilage type lacks a perichondrium?
Back: Fibrocartilage.

Front: Ch 7: What is a lacuna?
Back: The space in the cartilage matrix that houses a chondrocyte.

Front: Ch 7: Appositional versus interstitial growth?
Back: Appositional adds cartilage at the surface from the perichondrium and increases width; interstitial divides chondrocytes inside lacunae and increases length.

Front: Ch 7: How is cartilage nourished?
Back: By diffusion from synovial fluid or from vessels in the perichondrium — cartilage is avascular.

Front: Ch 7: What are the two layers of perichondrium?
Back: An outer fibrous layer of collagen and an inner chondrogenic layer of cells.

Front: Ch 13: Where does hemopoiesis occur in the adult?
Back: Red marrow of the axial skeleton — vertebrae, ribs, sternum, pelvis, and proximal femur.

Front: Ch 13: What is a proerythroblast?
Back: The first recognizable erythroid precursor: large, with lacy chromatin, nucleoli, and basophilic cytoplasm.

Front: Ch 13: What is a reticulocyte?
Back: A young erythrocyte that has extruded its nucleus but still contains residual RNA.

Front: Ch 13: How does a megakaryocyte make platelets?
Back: It becomes polyploid with a lobulated nucleus; its cytoplasm fragments into platelets.

Front: Ch 13: Name the granulocyte maturation sequence.
Back: Myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte → metamyelocyte → band cell → segmented cell.

Front: Ch 13: At which stage do specific granules first appear?
Back: The myelocyte stage (azurophilic granules appear earlier, at the promyelocyte stage).

Front: Ch 13: What makes erythropoietin and what does it do?
Back: Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney; it stimulates erythroid proliferation and hemoglobin synthesis.

Front: Ch 13: What does G-CSF do?
Back: Stimulates granulocyte production and mobilization from marrow.

Front: Ch 13: Which cells form the marrow stroma?
Back: Reticular cells, macrophages, adipocytes, and endothelial cells — the hematopoietic niche.

Front: Ch 14: Which MHC class do CD8 T cells read?
Back: MHC class I.

Front: Ch 14: Which cells present antigen on MHC class II?
Back: Antigen-presenting cells: dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells.

Front: Ch 14: Where does positive selection of T cells occur?
Back: The thymic cortex.

Front: Ch 14: What is the function of Hassall corpuscles?
Back: Concentric medullary thymic epithelial structures; in humans they express TSLP and can influence dendritic-cell pathways linked to regulatory T-cell development. Their full in-vivo roles remain under study.

Front: Ch 14: What is the white pulp of the spleen?
Back: Lymphoid tissue around central arteries — periarteriolar T-cell sheaths and B-cell follicles.

Front: Ch 14: Why does the spleen need no afferent lymphatics?
Back: It filters blood, not lymph; antigens arrive in the blood.

Front: Ch 15: Which cells of the stomach secrete hydrochloric acid?
Back: Parietal cells — they have intracellular canaliculi and abundant mitochondria.

Front: Ch 15: Which cells secrete pepsinogen?
Back: Chief (zymogenic) cells of the gastric glands.

Front: Ch 15: What are Brunner glands and where are they?
Back: Mucous glands in the duodenal submucosa.

Front: Ch 15: What is the function of Paneth cells?
Back: Secrete lysozyme and defensins at the base of intestinal crypts — innate defense.

Front: Ch 15: Where are Peyer patches and what are they?
Back: Lymphoid follicles in the ileal lamina propria and submucosa.

Front: Ch 16: Which salivary gland is purely serous?
Back: The parotid.

Front: Ch 16: What do striated ducts do?
Back: Reabsorb sodium and chloride and add bicarbonate, making saliva hypotonic.

Front: Ch 16: What do centroacinar cells secrete?
Back: Bicarbonate-rich fluid; they are the first cells of the pancreatic duct, inside the acinus.

Front: Ch 16: Secretin versus CCK?
Back: Secretin stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic fluid; CCK stimulates enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.

Front: Ch 16: Name the portal triad.
Back: Portal venule, hepatic arteriole, and bile ductule (with a lymphatic), in the portal area.

Front: Ch 16: Which way does bile flow in a hepatic lobule?
Back: Toward the portal area — opposite to the direction of blood flow.

Front: Ch 16: What are Kupffer cells?
Back: Macrophages attached to the sinusoidal endothelium of the liver.

Front: Ch 16: What do Ito (hepatic stellate) cells store?
Back: Vitamin A, in lipid droplets; they also produce collagen in fibrosis.

Front: Ch 16: Where are bile canaliculi?
Back: Between adjacent hepatocytes, sealed by tight junctions.

Front: Ch 16: What does the gallbladder do?
Back: Stores and concentrates bile by absorbing water; CCK contracts it.

Front: Ch 21: What forms the blood–testis barrier and what does it separate?
Back: Tight junctions between Sertoli cells; a basal compartment with spermatogonia and an adluminal compartment with spermatocytes and spermatids.

Front: Ch 21: Name three Sertoli cell secretions.
Back: Androgen-binding protein, inhibin, and Müllerian-inhibiting substance (also transferrin and fluid).

Front: Ch 21: Which hormone drives Leydig cells?
Back: Luteinizing hormone (also called interstitial cell-stimulating hormone).

Front: Ch 21: How long does spermatogenesis take?
Back: About two months, from the last spermatogonial mitosis to spermatid formation.

Front: Ch 21: Which enzymes does the acrosome contain?
Back: Hyaluronidase and acrosin (a trypsin-like protease).

Front: Ch 21: What epithelium lines the epididymis?
Back: Pseudostratified columnar with principal cells bearing stereocilia and small basal cells.

Front: Ch 21: What are the muscle layers of the ductus deferens?
Back: Inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal — a very thick muscularis.

Front: Ch 21: How much of the ejaculate comes from the seminal vesicles?
Back: About 70% — fructose, prostaglandins, and fibrinogen.

Front: Ch 21: Name the three zones of the prostate.
Back: Peripheral (70%, cancer), central (25%), and transition (5%, benign hyperplasia).

Front: Ch 21: What causes erection?
Back: Parasympathetic acetylcholine → endothelial nitric oxide → cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation → helicine arteries dilate and cavernous spaces fill.

Front: Ch 22: Which cells aromatize androgens to estrogens?
Back: Granulosa cells, using androstenedione from theca interna cells.

Front: Ch 22: What is released at ovulation?
Back: A secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II, surrounded by the corona radiata.

Front: Ch 22: How is polyspermy prevented?
Back: Cortical granule exocytosis converts the zona pellucida into the impenetrable perivitelline barrier.

Front: Ch 22: Which hormone rescues the corpus luteum in early pregnancy?
Back: hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast.

Front: Ch 22: Proliferative versus secretory endometrium?
Back: Proliferative: straight narrow glands and mitoses. Secretory: tortuous dilated glands with secretion and edematous stroma.

Front: Ch 23: Name the five layers of the cornea in order.
Back: Corneal epithelium, Bowman membrane, stroma, Descemet membrane, and endothelium.

Front: Ch 23: Trace aqueous humor from production to drainage.
Back: Ciliary processes → posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork → scleral venous sinus.

Front: Ch 23: How is the lens nourished?
Back: By diffusion from the aqueous humor and vitreous — it is avascular.

Front: Ch 23: Rods versus cones?
Back: Rods contain rhodopsin and work in dim light; cones support color and detailed vision. The central foveola is rod-free, although the peripheral fovea can contain a few rods.

Front: Ch 23: Why is the fovea the site of highest acuity?
Back: The central foveola has densely packed cones and laterally displaced inner retinal layers, enabling high-acuity vision; the surrounding foveal periphery can contain rods.

Front: Ch 23: Why is the optic disc a blind spot?
Back: Ganglion cell axons converge there to form the optic nerve; there are no photoreceptors.

Front: Ch 23: Name three functions of the retinal pigment epithelium.
Back: Absorbs stray light; forms the blood–retina barrier; phagocytoses shed discs and regenerates 11-cis-retinal.

Front: Ch 23: Name the retinal layers from the vitreous inward.
Back: Inner limiting membrane, nerve fiber layer, ganglion cell layer, inner plexiform, inner nuclear, outer plexiform, outer nuclear, outer limiting, rod and cone layer, pigment epithelium.

Front: Ch 23: Endolymph versus perilymph?
Back: Endolymph is high in potassium and fills the membranous labyrinth; perilymph resembles CSF and fills the bony labyrinth.

Front: Ch 23: Which cells transduce sound in the organ of Corti?
Back: Hair cells — about 12,000 outer cells in three to five rows and 3,500 inner cells in one row.

Front: Ch 23: Macula versus crista?
Back: Maculae (utricle and saccule) detect gravity and linear acceleration; cristae (semicircular ducts) detect rotational acceleration.

Front: Ch 23: What does the tectorial membrane do?
Back: It overlies the organ of Corti and its tallest stereocilia are embedded in it, so basilar membrane movement bends the hair bundles.
